enonce_intro_markdown:
**Section C : Comprehension**

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. Use complete sentences and use your own words.

All around me, I see people falling in love, walking in love, growing with the love they have found - and it accentuates loneliness. For here I am, having conceived two children, given one away, about to bear another alone. And all I ever wanted was love. All I ever longed for was a home and strong arms to hold me so I could sleep through the night. I wanted someone who would be there with me to meet the morning.

When I was 15, I never thought the next nine years would bring me such despair, emptiness and sorrow. Now at 24, I am still alone. While you are waiting for love to come to you, I have destroyed the hope of waiting because I was never willing to wait. I was so hungry for love that I tried to taste it all too early, too fast and now there is little left.

You cannot sell in the game of love and win. To compare it with playing cards, once you've played your ace - given whole self - the game is over; and if ever you want to play again, you will have to play with a worn deck, but with a new partner. The deck gets pretty shabby looking after a while and you will be sad because it is the only deck you have. And if your "king" turns out to be a joker, you pick up the cards and berate yourself for being so blind.

The agony becomes even more real when you see that things could have been very different. If you had known the rules to play by, you might have lost the king you thought you wanted, but your deck would have stayed intact, beautiful, indeed a king could be.

The fear you feel when you love someone and say "No" to him, and the pain that could come if he leaves you for saying "No" seems awesome and devastating to you now - but the greater pain comes when you say "Yes" and he tires of you, calling you "not the kind of girl he wants to marry". You may choose not to believe me, but it is true.

A man who truly loves you will not ask for your body first. He will ask if you will marry him. He will ask to be the one to provide for you and meet your needs so you can give him in all truth and confidence the secret of your soul. He will see the sacred beauty of your gift and will handle it with the gentleness of the man beholding the pearl he has sought for so long.

Value yourself, for you are very precious. Don't sell out. Any price you're given less than a love willing to commit itself - that price is too cheap. Waiting may seem very hard for you. You think so because you are young and still carry the impatience of a child. Learn patience; it is the beginning of self-discipline, a lesson that must be learned sooner or later. The sooner you learn it, the greater the joy, the lesser you sorrow. I know I have to learn it now, and I wish I had learned it then ...

*(Culled from the Christian Reader vol.13 N°1, January/February 1975)*

questions.enonce_markdown: Mention any two things the writer notices around her.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Une question de compréhension "mention any two things" demande de repérer une information explicite dans le texte, puis de la reformuler avec ses propres mots plutôt que de recopier la phrase telle quelle - la consigne "use your own words" est notée par le correcteur.

Dans le premier paragraphe, la narratrice observe autour d'elle des gens qui tombent amoureux, qui vivent leur amour au quotidien, et dont l'amour grandit avec le temps. Deux réponses parmi les suivantes suffisent : (1) elle voit des gens tomber amoureux ("people falling in love") ; (2) elle voit des gens vivre leur amour au quotidien ("people walking in love") ; (3) elle voit des gens dont l'amour s'épanouit avec le temps ("people growing with the love they have found").

Réponse rédigée : *"Around her, the writer notices people falling in love and others whose love keeps growing stronger as time goes by."*

questions.enonce_markdown: What happened to the writer at the age of 15?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Quand une question porte sur un moment précis mentionné dans le texte, il faut relire attentivement la phrase qui contient ce repère temporel et comprendre ce qu'elle implique, même quand l'événement n'est pas décrit de façon totalement explicite.

Le texte indique : "When I was 15, I never thought the next nine years would bring me such despair, emptiness and sorrow." À 15 ans, la narratrice a commencé les expériences amoureuses qui allaient, au cours des neuf années suivantes, la conduire au désespoir, au vide et au chagrin - sans qu'elle s'y attende à l'époque.

Réponse rédigée : *"At the age of 15, the writer started living out her search for love, never imagining that the following nine years would bring her so much despair, emptiness and sorrow instead of happiness."*

questions.enonce_markdown: Mention any two consequences mentioned in the text on a girl who easily says "Yes" to a man.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Pour une question "mention any two consequences", il faut localiser dans le texte le passage qui traite explicitement de la conséquence, puis en extraire deux éléments distincts plutôt que de reformuler deux fois la même idée.

Le texte précise : "the greater pain comes when you say 'Yes' and he tires of you, calling you 'not the kind of girl he wants to marry'." Deux conséquences distinctes apparaissent : (1) l'homme se lasse d'elle ("he tires of you") ; (2) il lui dit qu'elle n'est pas le genre de fille qu'il veut épouser ("not the kind of girl he wants to marry"), c'est-à-dire qu'il refuse de l'épouser.

Réponse rédigée : *"When a girl easily says 'Yes' to a man, he may grow tired of her, and he may end up telling her that she is not the kind of girl he wants to marry."*

questions.enonce_markdown: How does a man who really loves you behave?
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Cette question porte sur un paragraphe entier consacré à un seul sujet ("a man who truly loves you") : il faut rassembler plusieurs informations réparties dans ce paragraphe plutôt que de n'en retenir qu'une seule.

Le texte décrit un homme qui : ne demande pas d'abord le corps de la femme ("will not ask for your body first") ; lui demande de l'épouser ("He will ask if you will marry him") ; veut être celui qui subvient à ses besoins ("provide for you and meet your needs") ; traite la relation avec délicatesse et respect, comme un homme qui découvre enfin la perle précieuse qu'il cherchait depuis longtemps.

Réponse rédigée : *"A man who really loves you does not ask for your body first; he asks you to marry him, wants to provide for your needs, and treats you with great gentleness and respect, as something truly precious."*

questions.enonce_markdown: What advice does the writer give young people? Is it necessary? Justify.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Une question en deux temps ("What... ? Is it necessary? Justify.") exige deux réponses distinctes et articulées : d'abord identifier l'information demandée dans le texte, puis prendre position et justifier cette position en s'appuyant sur des éléments du texte, pas seulement sur une opinion personnelle non étayée.

Dans le dernier paragraphe, la narratrice conseille aux jeunes de se valoriser ("Value yourself, for you are very precious"), de ne pas se brader ("Don't sell out") et d'apprendre la patience, qui est le début de la discipline personnelle ("Learn patience; it is the beginning of self-discipline"). Ce conseil est nécessaire : la narratrice elle-même a souffert de ne pas avoir attendu ("I was so hungry for love that I tried to taste it all too early") et regrette de ne pas avoir appris la patience plus tôt ("I wish I had learned it then") - son propre témoignage prouve que l'impatience mène à la souffrance, alors que la patience mène à davantage de joie et moins de chagrin.

Réponse rédigée : *"The writer advises young people to value themselves, not to give themselves away cheaply, and to learn patience. This advice is necessary because her own experience shows that rushing into love too early only brought her despair, while learning patience would have spared her that pain."*
